title: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium
summary: Exfiltration over a physical medium is theft in which data leaves on hardware instead of over the network: a removable drive, an external disk, a phone, a media player, or any other portable device that can store or forward files. It is the natural choice where the network offers no way out, most obviously on an air-gapped estate, and it can serve either as the final exit point or as a bridge that moves data between systems that are not connected to each other. The activity is dangerous precisely because it bypasses network monitoring, and it is often paired with staging and compression so the data fits on a small device, and with copying that looks like routine file opening on the endpoint. The artefacts are largely local and physical: device connection and removal records, driver installation for new hardware, volume mount events, file copies to removable paths, sudden changes in file timestamps and sizes on a staging folder, and in mature environments physical access logs and media registers. Detection combines endpoint telemetry with policy: blocked or allow-listed device classes, alerts on write activity to removable media, and investigation of any removable device attached to a system that handles sensitive data.

beginner.definition: This means taking data out of a building on a physical device instead of sending it over the network. The device could be a memory stick, an external disk, a phone or a music player. Attackers use it when the network is closed or well watched.
beginner.whyItMatters: Network monitoring cannot see data that leaves in a pocket. A memory stick can hold a huge amount of information. One person with physical access is enough, and visitors or contractors may bring their own device. If nobody records what is plugged in, the theft may never be noticed.
howItWorks: The attacker gathers and compresses the files they want on the victim computer.
A removable device is attached, and the system may install a driver for it.
The data is copied to the device, which creates file access and write activity on the host.
The device is then removed, and the copied data physically leaves the site in a pocket.
On disconnected networks the same device can carry data between separate systems.
In some cases a device that pretends to be a keyboard is used to run commands automatically.
beginner.example: Imagine a hospital records office with no internet connection at all. Nobody can email a file out. A cleaner with a key to the office brings a small memory stick in a coat pocket, copies a folder of patient letters, and walks out. Every network alarm in the building stayed silent, because nothing left by the network.
takeaways: Removable media bypasses network defences completely, so endpoint policy matters more than firewalls.
Record device connection events and alert on writes to removable storage.
Protect the most sensitive data with encryption and strict access, so a lost device is less damaging.

objectives: Explain why an adversary chooses a physical medium instead of a network channel.
Describe how data is staged, copied and carried out on a removable device.
Identify endpoint artefacts such as device connection and file write records.
Explain the specific risk this technique poses to air-gapped or segmented networks.
Recommend device control and media handling policies that reduce the exposure.
